pairs.rationale: The Ephesian city secretary dismisses the assembly after warning about the day's uproar; the next stage begins after that uproar ceases and Paul leaves for Macedonia. This is the narrative transition from the same disturbance, not an independent report of its conclusion.

Paul's earlier plan names travel through Macedonia and Achaia before Jerusalem; the subsequent narrative reports encouragement through Macedonia and arrival in Greece. This connects the plan with its travel stages without making the place lists identical or supplying unrecorded dates.

In Damascus a plot to kill Saul leads to escape by the wall; here a plot as Paul prepares to sail changes his route to Macedonia. Both describe opposition altering his movements, but the groups, locations and escape methods differ; this verse does not itself specify every plot detail.

Aristarchus is named as a Thessalonian companion here and later as a Macedonian from Thessalonica accompanying the voyage. The identification concerns this named companion, not independent confirmation of the entire list or identification of Gaius of Derbe with another Gaius.

The companions go ahead and wait in Troas; the following travel report says that we came to them there. This is an explicit waiting-and-rejoining sequence, without naming the first-person narrator or independently confirming every companion's movements.

The arrival at Troas rejoins the men previously said to be waiting there. This internal callback explains to them; the earlier notice does not independently verify the festival date, five-day crossing or seven-day stay.

The gathering's intended bread breaking and prolonged speaking are resumed after the interruption, when Paul breaks bread, eats and talks until dawn. These are stages of the same gathering, not a second independent testimony or a rule inferred for every Church meeting.

Eutychus is picked up dead after the fall, whereas the episode ends with the boy brought away alive. This explicit death/life contrast belongs to one narrative; it does not independently verify the height or replace dead with an unreported diagnosis.

Paul falls upon and embraces Eutychus before announcing life in him; Elisha prays and makes bodily contact with the dead child before the child's restoration. The bodily-contact restoration motif is comparable, while the actions, words and individuals differ; Elisha's prayer and particular movements are not inserted into Paul's scene.

Paul's bread breaking and continued conversation fulfil the gathering's stated purpose and extend the address beyond its earlier midnight point to dawn. This recalls the same meeting, not another first-day meal or an independent account of every action.

The conclusion that the boy is brought away alive answers the earlier report that Eutychus was picked up dead. The link preserves the narrator's two descriptions and the resulting comfort, without explaining away the earlier dead wording.

The party sails ahead intending to collect Paul at Assos while he intends to travel on foot; the next notice records meeting him at Assos and taking him aboard. This is a specific arrangement followed by its narrated execution.

The Assos meeting and boarding follow the previously stated plan that the others would sail ahead and Paul would go on foot. Mitylene is the next reported destination, not a place named in the earlier arrangement.

The sailing sequence ends at Miletus, and the following action begins from Miletus when Paul summons the Ephesian elders. This identifies the speech's narrative staging point; it does not independently verify Chios, Samos or the individual sailing days.

Paul's stated aim is Jerusalem, if possible by Pentecost; the later narrative records arrival in Jerusalem. The arrival connects with the destination, but it does not itself date arrival to Pentecost or prove that the intended deadline was met.

The people summoned from Ephesus are the Church's elders; the charge to this audience describes their oversight and shepherding responsibility. This identifies the speech's audience and role language, without supplying a later system of offices or another appointment ceremony.

Paul appeals to the Ephesian hearers' knowledge of his conduct among them; the letter appeals to its hearers as witnesses of the missionaries' labor and conduct. The public appeal to remembered ministry is comparable, while the communities and the letter's plural speakers differ.

Paul describes service marked by tears and trials; the letter describes writing out of much affliction and anguish with many tears. Both portray tearful apostolic ministry, but the letter's writing occasion does not independently verify the plots or humility described in the Asian ministry.

The assertion that Paul did not hold back beneficial teaching is repeated as not holding back the whole purpose of God. These are complementary claims within the same farewell speech, not independent proof of every public or household lesson.

The farewell names repentance toward God and faith in Jesus for Jews and Greeks; Paul's later defense describes announcing repentance and turning to God across Jewish regions and among Gentiles. The repentance and broad mission scope correspond, while the geographical list, deeds clause and explicit faith wording differ.

Paul says he is bound in spirit and going to Jerusalem; at Tyre the disciples tell him through the Spirit not to set foot there. The comparison preserves these different formulations and the apparent tension, rather than changing the prohibition into merely a warning or deciding the lowercase spirit expression beyond the supplied wording.

The repeated Holy Spirit testimony about coming bonds and afflictions has a specific later counterpart in Agabus's belt sign and forecast of binding and Gentile custody. The general summary and the named prophecy have different scope; their wording is not made identical to every subsequent arrest action.

Paul resolves to complete his course and ministry; the letter uses the retrospective image of having finished the course and kept the faith. The shared course metaphor connects resolve and claimed completion without fixing the two passages to one occasion or equating every metaphorical detail.

The farewell assertion that the hearers will not see Paul's face again is explicitly recalled as the chief cause of their grief. The later verse records their response to his words, not independent verification of the whole future itinerary.

Paul grounds his claim to be clean from everyone's blood in having declared God's whole purpose in the following verse. Ezekiel's watchman is accountable for blood when he fails to warn, while warning rescues his own life. This is possible watchman background for Paul's responsibility language, not a verbatim quotation or an assertion that every commission detail is identical.

The statement that Paul did not hold back the whole purpose of God resumes his earlier claim not to withhold beneficial instruction. The repeated wording supports the speech's claim of completeness, while it remains one speaker's account rather than an independent audit of his teaching.

The elders are charged with attending to the flock and shepherding the Church; Peter's exhortation likewise addresses elders and the shepherding of God's flock. The leadership-and-flock responsibility is shared, while the commands and grounds differ; the letter does not repeat the acquired-through-blood clause or independently attest these overseers' placement.

Paul warns of fierce wolves entering and harming the flock; Jesus warns of false prophets in sheep's clothing who inwardly are ravenous wolves. Both use predatory wolf imagery for danger to the faithful, but the farewell's after-my-departure timing and Matthew's disguise are not transferred between passages.

Paul warns that men from within the hearers will speak distorted things and draw disciples after themselves; the letter warns of false teachers among its audience, fabricated words and many following their debaucheries. Both describe dangerous influence from within, while the followed objects and additional charges differ; the groups are not identified as one.

Paul recalls admonishing each person persistently; the letter recalls treating each hearer as a father does children, encouraging, comforting and solemnly urging them to walk worthily of God. The individual pastoral attention corresponds; the letter does not corroborate the farewell's three years, tears or every night and day.

Paul entrusts the elders to God and the word of His grace, able to build up and give an inheritance among the sanctified. His reported commission likewise offers an allotted share among those sanctified by faith in Jesus. Both connect a share with the sanctified community, while the speakers and wording differ.

Paul denies coveting anyone's valuables; the letter denies a pretext for greed and invokes God as witness. Both reject financial exploitation in ministry, but the letter's formulation does not independently verify the particular silver, gold or clothing list.

Paul says these hands served his own and his companions' needs; the letter says we toil, working with our own hands. The explicit manual-labor motif is shared, while the plural letter does not independently identify all the Ephesian beneficiaries or a particular trade.

Paul's example joins labor to supporting the weak; the letter tells the one who steals to stop, labor with his hands and have something to share with the needy. Both connect work with supplying others, without calling Paul a thief or presenting the letter as another verbatim record of Jesus' quoted giving saying.

Paul and the elders kneel and pray at their departure; the later Tyre farewell also includes kneeling prayer with the believers on the beach. The posture and farewell setting correspond, but the locations and participating groups differ.

The elders weep, embrace Paul's neck and kiss him; Joseph's reunion includes neck embraces, weeping and kisses among his brothers. The affectionate gestures form a bounded narrative comparison, with different actors and a farewell rather than a reunion or the same reconciliation history.

Their grief explicitly concerns the earlier statement that they would not see Paul's face again. This internal recollection identifies the words causing sorrow; accompanying him to the ship is the present farewell action, not proof about all subsequent meetings.

The departure after tearing themselves away follows the elders' weeping embrace and escort to the ship. This identifies the people and farewell behind the transition, without independently verifying the newly listed Cos, Rhodes and Patara stops.

The party boards a ship crossing to Phoenicia; the following voyage notice records reaching Tyre, where that ship was to unload cargo. This is a planned crossing followed by its narrated landing, not a separate confirmation of every maritime detail.

The arrival at Tyre continues the crossing on the ship just found for Phoenicia. The internal connection identifies the vessel and voyage stage; the earlier boarding notice does not corroborate the side on which Cyprus was passed or the cargo unloading.

The Tyrian disciples tell Paul through the Spirit not to enter Jerusalem, whereas Paul had said he was bound in spirit and going there. These different statements remain intact; the link does not silently turn the disciples' prohibition into only a prediction or force one interpretation of spirit in Paul's earlier words.

The Tyrian farewell names wives and children among the escort and then reports kneeling prayer on the beach; the Miletus farewell has Paul kneel with the elders and pray. The shared departure prayer connects, without merging the groups, assigning the earlier prayer to a beach or resolving the scope of the later we beyond the narration.

The Tyrian believers part from the voyagers at their boarding, comparable to the Ephesian elders accompanying Paul to the ship in the earlier farewell. The later report alone specifies the local people's return home; the two groups and ports remain distinct.

Philip is identified here as one of the seven; the earlier selection names Philip among the seven presented to the apostles. This supplies the explicit antecedent for his designation, not an identification with every other Philip or a claim that all seven share the later evangelist title.

Philip's daughters prophesy; the Pentecost citation explicitly includes daughters and female slaves among those who will prophesy. This is a concrete female-prophecy correspondence, without independently confirming four daughters, their virginity, or claiming this family exhausts the cited promise.

Agabus appears earlier among prophets arriving from Jerusalem and foretells famine through the Spirit; here the named prophet comes from Judea and gives another prediction. The recurring named prophet is connected, while the journeys, audiences and predictions remain different.

Agabus forecasts binding by the Jews and handing into Gentile hands; the subsequent narration has the crowd seize and drag Paul and the Roman tribune order him bound with two chains. Bonds and Gentile custody are connected, but the stated agents remain distinct: the narrative does not say the Jewish crowd tied the chains or voluntarily delivered him to the rescuing troops.

After Agabus's warning, the party and local people urge Paul not to go to Jerusalem; the Tyrian disciples had also told him not to enter. These are distinct groups and occasions; the earlier through-the-Spirit wording is preserved rather than attributed automatically to every later plea.

Paul declares readiness for bonds and death for Jesus' name, matching the earlier resolve not to value his own life above completing the ministry from Jesus. This is continuing personal resolve on the journey, not proof that a death in Jerusalem will occur.

The companions cease arguing and submit to the Lord's will; Jesus' prayer submits His own will to the Father's. The submission formula is comparable, but the speakers, prayers and decisions differ; the companions are not made the speakers of Jesus' cup petition.

The party now prepares and goes up toward Jerusalem, the destination Paul had previously declared. This is the onward movement of the stated journey, without making the preparations an independent arrival report or resolving the different Spirit-related instructions.

Paul and his party are gladly received in Jerusalem; the earlier visit also records reception by the Jerusalem Church and its leaders. This is a repeated reception setting at different visits, not the same council meeting or an identity imposed on every welcoming brother.

Paul meets James and the elders in Jerusalem; the earlier council scene also has the elders gathered and James speaking after Peter and the missionaries. The link locates James within recurring Jerusalem leadership, without equating the visits, importing an apostle list into this meeting or identifying him with the James already killed.

Paul reports what God has done among Gentiles through his ministry; the earlier Antioch report by Paul and Barnabas recounts what God did with them and the opened door of faith for Gentiles. The mission-report pattern and divine agency correspond, with different hearers, visits and reporting personnel.

The Jerusalem speakers describe many Jewish believers as zealous for the law; the earlier council includes believing Pharisees who demand Gentile circumcision and law observance. Both show law commitment among believers, but this verse does not identify all the Jerusalem believers as Pharisees or say they all make that Gentile demand.

The report alleges that Paul tells diaspora Jews not to circumcise their children; the earlier narrative records Paul circumcising Timothy because of local Jews. This is a contrasting concrete action, not a transfer of Timothy's age or mixed parentage to the rumored children's case, nor independent proof concerning every alleged teaching.

The four men have a vow, and the following instructions involve purification and shaved heads; Numbers gives the law's setting for vowed consecration and hair restrictions. This is scriptural background, not an assertion that Acts explicitly names their vow type or that every Numbers condition is independently narrated here.

The proposed expenses and head shaving connect with Numbers' completion rites involving offerings and the consecrated person's shaved hair. Acts has Paul assist the four men and purify with them; it does not say here that Paul shaves his own head or that every tent-based legal detail is reproduced in the temple arrangement.

The Jerusalem speakers recall the sent decision for Gentile believers and its four requirements, corresponding to the council letter's decree. This is an explicit internal recall; sent word is retained, and no new circumcision requirement or complete Mosaic-law obligation is added to the listed provisions.

The narrative places Paul purified in the temple with offerings in view; his later defense says that he brought alms and offerings and was found purified there. This is a retrospective report of the same setting, not independent testimony that every planned offering had already been completed before the disturbance.

Asian Jews see Paul in the temple and initiate the disturbance; Paul's later defense identifies Jews from Asia in connection with being found purified there. The shared group and setting connect the accounts without treating the defense as an independent witness to the seven-day count or every crowd action.

The charges against Paul name the people, law and holy place; Stephen's accusers likewise allege speech against the holy place and law and altered Mosaic customs. These are comparable accusation patterns, not endorsements of their truth; the Greek-entry allegation belongs to Paul's scene, not Stephen's.

Trophimus appears earlier among Paul's companions from Asia and is here identified more specifically as Ephesian. This connects the named companion; the actual observation is in the city, while his entry into the temple remains the accusers' supposition, not an independently narrated act.

The earlier narrative records seizure in the temple and the attempt on Paul's life in the following verse; his later defense recalls the Jews seizing him in the temple and trying to kill him. This is Paul's retrospective reference, not a second independent eyewitness account or proof of every motive he gives in the speech.

The threat to kill Paul and the tribune's intervention are later summarized in Lysias's letter as seizure, imminent death and rescue. The letter's connection with learning Roman status is kept distinct from the narrative, which reveals that information during the later intended scourging episode; no unreported earlier disclosure is inserted.

Military intervention stops the crowd’s beating of Paul; the tribune later orders troops to remove him from a dangerously divided council. These are separate interventions by the military, with different groups and stages; fear of his being torn apart is not rewritten as a completed injury.

The tribune's order binding Paul is recalled when he becomes afraid on learning Paul is Roman and that he had bound him. This is the internal consequence of the same custody, not independent confirmation of two chains or a claim that he already knew the citizenship at the original arrest.

Both uproars include some shouting one thing and some another, making the crowd's activity confused. Ephesus concerns the Artemis disturbance, Jerusalem the temple accusation; the formula does not identify the crowds or transfer the Ephesian participants' motives to Jerusalem.

The soldiers have to carry Paul because of the crowd's violence; the later council dispute likewise prompts the tribune to have troops snatch him away for protection. The removal under threat corresponds, but the later scene does not independently attest the steps, carrying or a disabling injury.

The crowd cries for Paul to be taken away, comparable to the cry to remove Jesus before Pilate. The hostile removal demand is shared, while the accused men, officials and occasions differ; the demand to release Barabbas is not inserted into Paul's scene.

Paul first asks to speak to the tribune, who then asks him about Greek. In21:39 Paul explicitly asks to address the people, and21:40 grants that later request and records the Hebrew address. This connects the exchange’s stages without making the initial private question the same request as the subsequent public-speech permission.

The tribune's question suggests an Egyptian insurgent identity; Paul's reply identifies him instead as a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia. The suspicion remains the official's question, not a narrated identification of Paul with that Egyptian or the Sicarii.

Paul repeats his Jewish identity and Tarsus/Cilicia origin in the ensuing defense, adding his upbringing and education. The repeated origin does not make Tarsian civic identity proof of Roman citizenship or establish the tribune's earlier suspicion.

The permission, hand gesture and Hebrew opening lead to the crowd becoming still quieter on hearing that language. This is the continuation of one address; the supplied Hebrew wording is preserved rather than silently replaced by another language name.

Paul's men, brothers and fathers opening recalls Stephen's address to his hearers before his defense. The formal appeal to an audience corresponds, but the assemblies, speakers and ensuing arguments are different; no identity of the two hearings is claimed.

The crowd's increased quiet responds to the Hebrew speech just introduced after Paul's hand signal. This is the same speech's continuation, without changing Hebrew to a different language designation or treating the repeated report as an independent account.

Paul names Gamaliel as his teacher in the ancestral law; the earlier narrative identifies Gamaliel as a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law. That gives the named teacher's narrative antecedent, without independently verifying Paul's classroom history or identifying Gamaliel with every later Pharisaic speaker.

Paul's confession of imprisoning men and women recalls Saul entering houses and dragging both men and women to prison. This is the same persecutor's retrospective account; the earlier selected verse does not itself detail every death implied by the defense's to-the-point-of-death statement.

The defense's letters and Damascus mission to bring prisoners back to Jerusalem recall Saul asking the high priest for letters to Damascus synagogues to bind people of the Way. The reports correspond in authorization and purpose, with different wording and no claim that the council is currently testifying in the narrative.

Both defenses place the heavenly-light encounter on the Damascus journey at noon. The Agrippa speech further describes light brighter than the sun around Paul and his companions; those details are not silently added to this verse or taken as separate eyewitness testimony.

Paul's fall and the repeated Saul, Saul persecution question recall the earlier Damascus narration. This is another presentation of the same event, not an independently named witness or a statement that every companion's posture is described identically.

The question about the Lord's identity and the answer identifying Jesus recur in the earlier narration. The defense explicitly includes the Nazarene designation, which the selected earlier answer does not; the two quotations are not made word-for-word identical.

The companion reports differ: the narration says they heard the voice and saw no one; the defense says they saw the light but did not hear the voice of the One speaking to Paul. Both formulations are preserved, without replacing hear with understand or supplying an unreported sequence to harmonize them.

Both reports command Saul to rise, enter Damascus/the city and await instructions about what he is to do. The defense includes Paul's question and appointed wording; these are not inserted into the earlier report as though its supplied text contained them.

Paul's inability to see and being led by hand into Damascus repeat the earlier blindness-and-leading report. The defense supplies the brightness explanation; the earlier verse does not state that cause in the same words or resolve the companion-hearing difference.

The named Ananias of Damascus is earlier introduced as a disciple receiving a vision; the defense describes his law devotion and good reputation among local Jews. The complementary descriptions do not make him the later high priest Ananias or independently verify every reputation claim.

Ananias addresses Brother Saul and sight returns promptly in both reports. The earlier narration includes laying on hands and the scale-like falling description; the defense has regain-your-sight words and looking at Ananias at that hour. Their actions and timing expressions remain distinct.

Ananias announces God's appointment for Saul to know, see and hear; the earlier scene has the Lord tell Ananias that Saul is a chosen instrument who will bear His name. The calling corresponds, but the recipient of the earlier divine speech and the wording are different; these are not one identical quotation.

The defense through Ananias commissions Paul as witness to what he has seen and heard; the Agrippa speech reports Jesus appointing him servant and witness to what he has seen and future appearances. The witness role corresponds while the speakers, settings and seen/heard versus future wording remain different.

Ananias joins baptism, washing away sins and invoking Jesus' name; the letter says you washed yourselves clean, were sanctified and were justified in the Lord Jesus Christ's name and in God's Spirit. The washing and name language correspond, preserving the letter's self-washing wording; it does not narrate Saul's baptism or repeat the command sequence as a formula.

Paul describes praying in the temple and falling into a trance; Peter's recap describes praying in Joppa and seeing a vision in a trance. Prayer and trance are associated in both, but the men, locations and visions differ and no identical sequence beyond their actual wording is imposed.

The defense reports a temple vision ordering departure because the testimony will not be accepted; the earlier account reports opposition and a killing attempt followed by the brothers sending Saul away. These related departure accounts give different reported agents and details; the earlier account does not independently narrate the vision or say every Jerusalem believer rejected him.

Paul recalls imprisoning and beating believers in synagogues; the Agrippa defense likewise recalls repeated punishment in synagogues and efforts to compel blasphemy. The persecution setting is shared, but the further rage, foreign-city and compelled-blasphemy details are not inserted into this verse.

The defense recalls Stephen's killing, Saul's approval and his guarding the killers' garments; the earlier narrative places garments at Saul's feet and states his consent to the killing. These are linked presentations within Acts, not independent verification of every quoted description.

The temple vision sends Paul far away to Gentiles; the Damascus commission in the Agrippa speech also includes sending him to Gentiles. The mission corresponds, but the visions are not collapsed into one occasion or made identical in their geographical and explanatory wording.

The renewed demand to remove Paul from the earth follows his Gentile-mission statement and recalls the earlier crowd's away-with-him cry. This is escalating hostility in successive stages, not an attribution of that demand to all Jewish believers or every earlier hearer.

Both hostile crowds shout and move garments in scenes involving Stephen and Paul; Saul had stood on the persecuting side in Stephen's scene. The contrast preserves different actions: Stephen is stoned, while this verse has garments flung and dust thrown, without narrating Paul being stoned here or identifying a particular ritual for the gestures.

Roman authorities order bodily punishment amid opposition to Paul in both scenes. Philippi has magistrates order rods and the beating carried out; here the tribune orders examination by scourging, which the following citizenship challenge interrupts. The officials, purposes, instruments and outcomes are not made identical.

Paul challenges punishment of an uncondemned Roman citizen, as his earlier Philippian protest invokes uncondemned Roman status after a public beating. The legal-status appeal recurs, but this challenge precedes the intended scourging, whereas the Philippian protest follows punishment and speaks in the plural.

The centurion passes Paul's Roman-citizenship objection to the tribune after hearing it. This is the transmission of the just-stated claim, not an independent account of the source or purchase price of Paul's citizenship.

The tribune directly asks Paul to confirm the Roman status already raised in his question to the centurion. The reply confirms Paul's stated claim within the interview; it does not itself give an independent documentary history of citizenship.

The tribune becomes afraid after learning Paul's Roman status, as the Philippian magistrates became afraid on hearing that the men were Romans. The response to the status claim corresponds, with different officials, plural versus singular citizens and different timing relative to punishment.

The narrative says the tribune convenes the council to learn the accusation; his letter later says he brought Paul to their council wishing to learn its reason. This is the official's later summary of the same action, not a separate hearing or independent acquittal.

Paul asserts a good conscience before God at the council and later says he strives for a blameless conscience toward God and people. These are related self-descriptions in separate defenses, not independent proof that every past action was right.

Paul is ordered struck on the mouth by the high priest; Jesus is struck by an officer during a high-priestly exchange and questions the blow. The hearing-and-blow motif corresponds, but the priests, victims, order and replies differ; Ananias is not identified with Jesus' interrogator.

Paul calls the judging high priest a whitewashed wall while exposing conduct contrary to the law; Jesus uses whitewashed tombs for outward appearance hiding uncleanness and lawlessness. The whitewash rebuke is comparable, but walls and tombs, addressees and specific charges differ; this is not a quotation or a narrated fulfilment of Paul's prediction.

Bystanders accuse Paul of insulting the high priest, while the officer who strikes Jesus challenges how He answers the high priest. The accusation about disrespect corresponds, without endorsing either accusation or treating the groups and blows as the same event.

Paul cites the ruler prohibition: Acts has a ruler of your people, whereas the supplied Exodus has rulers of your people. The earlier prohibition about gods is not part of his quotation. His statement that he did not know the man was high priest remains his claim, without supplying an unreported cause.

Paul identifies as Pharisaic and makes resurrection hope the issue; the Agrippa defense likewise recalls his Pharisaic life and frames the trial around ancestral promise and God's raising the dead. The arguments recur at different hearings, without turning the earlier council tactic into every prosecutor's agreed description.

The split between Pharisees and Sadducees develops into some Pharisaic scribes arguing in Paul's defense. This traces the same council dispute's development, without saying every Pharisee accepted every claim or that the council issued a unanimous verdict.

Both passages explicitly associate Sadducees with denial of resurrection. Acts additionally names angel and spirit and contrasts the Pharisees; those further distinctions are not attributed to Matthew's selected statement or expanded beyond Acts's supplied both wording.

Some Pharisaic scribes allow the possibility that a spirit or angel spoke to Paul; Gamaliel earlier warns that opposing the apostles could mean fighting God if their work is from God. Both interventions invoke possible divine agency, with different speakers and cases; the scribes are not identified as Gamaliel and neither conditional is turned into an unconditional confession.

The tribune again has troops remove Paul from dangerous opponents, here fearing the divided council may tear him apart. The earlier rescue is from the temple crowd and includes carrying him on the steps; those circumstances and any completed injury are not imported into the council scene.

The Lord assures Paul that he must testify in Rome; the later angelic message says he must stand before Caesar and encourages him during the voyage. The continuing assurance of the destination corresponds, but the Lord and the angel are distinguished and the shipboard promise about other passengers is not added to this scene.

The conspirators' curse-bound refusal to eat or drink until Paul's death is repeated in the nephew's warning to the tribune. This is the same plot relayed within the narrative, not an oath taken by every Jew or an independent report of what eventually happened to the plotters.

The more-than-forty count recurs in the warning about the same ambushers. It remains more than forty rather than exactly forty; the repetition does not supply their names or report that their fasting later killed them.

The oath already narrated is now announced by its makers to the chief priests and elders. The formulations neither eat nor drink and taste nothing remain distinct, and the report does not say every elder personally took the oath.

The proposed pretext of a more accurate council inquiry is repeated in the nephew's report, which also specifies tomorrow. This is the plotting request relayed as a warning, not proof that the tribune had agreed to it or that the purported inquiry was sincere.

The narrator identifies the informer as Paul's sister's son; his later private report supplies the ambush and council-pretext details. This connects the informer's discovery with its reported content, without giving him an unreported name, exact age or another identity such as Timothy.

Paul asks a centurion to take the young man to the tribune, and the following verse narrates that action with the centurion explaining Paul's request. This is a specific request and its execution, not separate independent evidence for the plot.

The centurion's statement that Paul asked him to bring the young man directly resumes the earlier request. Prisoner is the centurion's description in this report; the repeated message does not identify a different informer.

The tribune withdraws privately to hear the young man, then orders him not to disclose that he informed him. The private interview and confidentiality instruction belong to the same warning; no injury, secret political motive or name is inferred from taking him by the hand.

The nephew describes the proposed council request using the earlier plot's more-accurate-inquiry pretext. His report includes tomorrow; the comparison does not turn the conspirators' stated intention into an honest inquiry or assume the commander has consented.

The warning repeats the original curse, fasting, more-than-forty group and readiness to kill under a council pretext. This is the same conspiracy relayed to the commander, not another independent conspiracy or knowledge of the plotters' later fate.

The command not to disclose the informing concludes the private interview just introduced. This identifies the confidential exchange being protected, without inventing a subsequent disclosure or the informer's motive.

The night escort order is followed by the soldiers taking Paul by night and the horsemen continuing the next day. The execution of the escort is connected, but the later report does not independently repeat every number or the exact third-hour departure.

The commander orders safe conveyance to Felix, and the later arrival presents Paul and the letter to the governor. The delivery follows the stated destination; the arrival report does not independently count the mounts or say the tribune personally accompanied him.

Both passages introduce a written letter whose body follows in the narrative. The formal embedded-letter device is shared, while Lysias's custody dispatch and the Jerusalem council's Gentile instructions have different authors, recipients and authority; their contents are not conflated.

The letter addresses governor Felix as most excellent; Paul later uses the same honorific for Festus. This is a bounded formal-address parallel between different officials, not proof of their moral excellence or identity.

Lysias's letter links his rescue with having learned Paul was Roman; the narrative discloses the citizenship during the later intended-scourging episode. The differing presentation is kept intact without inserting earlier unreported knowledge or assigning an unreported motive for the letter's wording.

Lysias's letter says he brought Paul before the council to learn the accusation; the earlier narrative gives that stated purpose, summons and presentation. This is a retrospective summary of the same council appearance, not a second inquiry.

Lysias reports law-related questions rather than a charge deserving death or imprisonment; Festus later describes religious disputes and Jesus' being alive rather than the expected crimes. These are different officials' summaries with different addressees and scope, not a narrated release or identical charge lists.

The letter summarizes disclosure of the plot and the decision to send Paul onward; the prior scene supplies the young man's warning and the resulting escort orders. This is an official recap, not independent verification of every letter claim or proof that all accusers obeyed an order immediately.

The soldiers' night journey follows the command to prepare a nighttime escort toward Caesarea. Antipatris is the narrated intermediate stopping point here, not a replacement name for Caesarea or independent confirmation of the exact third hour.

The horsemen continuing with Paul were included in the earlier escort order. This identifies the continuing contingent while others return; the later verse does not repeat all numerical totals or identify each returning unit.

Presentation of Paul and delivery of the letter to the governor carry out the earlier conveyance order and written dispatch to Felix. This is the ordered transfer's outcome, not a new letter or an appearance by Lysias himself.

The governor learns that Paul is from Cilicia, the region Paul earlier named with his Tarsus origin. The regional identity corresponds, without turning this provincial inquiry into a new citizenship grant or inferring an unstated jurisdiction ruling.

The governor says he will hear Paul when the accusers arrive; the following episode records their arrival and presentation of the case. This connects the stated condition with the next hearing stage, not a final judgment or a recorded visit from Lysias.

The arrival of Ananias, elders and Tertullus supplies the accusers whose presence the governor had awaited. The earlier order does not independently confirm the five-day interval or identify every accompanying elder; this high priest Ananias is not the Damascus disciple.

Tertullus offers a favorable portrait of Felix's peace and reforms; the narrator later explicitly gives favor with the Jews as Felix's reason for leaving Paul bound. The two portrayals of the same official may be compared without treating the advocate's praise as narrator-certified fact or claiming that every alleged reform is disproved.

Tertullus's most excellent Felix address repeats the honorific and recipient in Lysias's letter. The formal courtesy corresponds, but neither expression independently certifies the governor's righteousness or the truth of the surrounding praise.

Tertullus asks the governor to hear briefly after his courteous opening; Paul's answering opening gives a different reason for confidence in addressing the same judge. These are opposed sides' introductions at one hearing, not the same speaker or a shared endorsement of every compliment.

The advocate alleges worldwide disturbance by Paul; the earlier Thessalonian accusation likewise portrays the missionaries as unsettling the world and opposing Caesar. This is a recurring hostile accusation pattern, not narrator endorsement; the Nazarene-party label and the specific earlier king charge remain distinct.

The accusation that Paul tried to profane the temple and was seized recalls the earlier defilement accusation and seizure.
